claim: The cache is safe to share between callers. A repeated lookup does not call the loader again, the entry dropped at capacity is the least recently used one, and a caller can change anything inside the rows it gets back without affecting later lookups.
why: Get returns list(items[key]), which copies only the outer list, so each row is still the object the cache holds. Appending to the result is harmless, but assigning into a row changes the cached row and every later lookup sees it. The README says each caller gets its own copy, which is true only one level deep.

deciding.note: the refuted part: inner rows are shared

root.claim: The cache is safe to share between callers. A repeated lookup does not call the loader again, the entry dropped at capacity is the least recently used one, and a caller can change anything inside the rows it gets back without affecting later lookups.

atoms.claim: A repeated lookup does not call the loader again
atoms.evidence: get() only calls the loader when the key is absent; main.py shows loads stays 2 on the repeat of a.

atoms.claim: The entry dropped at capacity is the least recently used one
atoms.evidence: A hit does move_to_end and eviction is popitem(last=False); after a, b, a, c the entry b is gone and a stays.

atoms.claim: A caller can change anything inside the returned rows without affecting later lookups
atoms.evidence: list() is a shallow copy. Running r = c.get('a'); r[0][1] = 99 makes the next c.get('a')[0] show 99.
